title: What is a good growth rate: investor benchmarks by stage (Lenny's survey of two dozen VCs)
summary: Lenny surveyed about two dozen top investors on what counts as good and great growth by stage. Early on, investors ignore small-base MoM percentages and watch time to $1M ARR, retention, and efficiency. For consumer, engagement and retention beat revenue. Most of the quotes are from the investors, not Lenny.

principles.text: Early-stage MoM growth percentages mean little because the base is tiny; investors want to see accelerating momentum instead.
principles.quote: In the early stages, investors don’t care about month-over-month growth

principles.text: If you need a sub-$1M ARR MoM benchmark, investors typically cited 15%-25% month over month.
principles.quote: if you’re looking for a month-over-month benchmark below $1m ARR, answers typically fell in the 15%-25% range.

principles.text: For early B2B, speed to $1M ARR after launch is the key metric: within 12 months is good, within 9 months is great.
principles.quote: getting to $1m ARR within a year of launch is GOOD, and getting there in three quarters (9 months) is GREAT.

principles.text: Launch strategically: weak traction after launch is worse than being pre-launch, since it signals a weak market or value prop.
principles.quote: For this reason, you want to be strategic about when you launch

principles.text: Without fast ARR growth, show that people want the product via high retention and efficiency.
principles.quote: Without fast ARR growth, you’ll need to show strong signals that people really want your product—through high retention and efficiency

principles.text: For early consumer products, engagement, virality and retention matter more than revenue.
principles.quote: for early-stage _consumer_ businesses, it’s all about intensity of engagement, virality, and retention—not revenue
